🎧 Listening

Listen to podcasts like *BBC Learning English, All Ears English, or The English We Speak.*

Watch movies or shows without subtitles (or with English subtitles first).

Try *TED Talks* — they’re perfect for advanced vocabulary.

🗣️ Speaking

Practice thinking in English every day.

Record yourself speaking about a topic for 1–2 minutes; then listen and correct mistakes.

Join online speaking clubs or practice with a teacher (like your classes 😉).

📖 Reading

*Read short news articles (The Guardian, The Economist, National Geographic).*

Move on to novels or essays — highlight new expressions and phrasal verbs.

✍️ Writing

*Keep a daily journal in Englis* h.

Write short essays or reflections about what you read or watch.

*Use advanced connectors* (e.g., however, nonetheless, as a result, in contrast).

🎯 Vocabulary & Grammar

Focus on collocations and idiomatic expressions.

Learn advanced grammar topics like inversion, cleft sentences, and mixed conditionals.

text: *Filler words* are the "social glue" of English. Native speakers use them to bridge ideas, soften a statement, or simply buy a few seconds of thinking time without creating an awkward silence.

1. *To Buy Time (Thinking Fillers)*
Use these when your brain needs a second to catch up with your mouth.

*Actually / Well:* Used to start a sentence when you're thinking or correcting something.

*"Well,* I haven’t really thought about it that way."

*Like:* Used mid-sentence (very common, but don't overdo it!).

"It was, like, the best coffee I’ve ever had."

*Let’s see / Let me think:* A very polite way to pause.

*"Let’s see* ... I think we met three years ago?"

1. Para ganar tiempo (Thinking Fillers)
Well... / Let’s see...: Bueno... / A ver...

Se usa al inicio de una frase para pensar la respuesta.

Actually: De hecho / En realidad.

Se usa para corregir algo o añadir información precisa.

Like: Como / O sea.

Es muy común entre nativos, se usa para comparar o cuando no encuentras la palabra exacta.

Let me think: Déjame pensar.

Una forma clara de pedir un segundo para procesar la idea.

2. *To Soften a Statement (Politeness Fillers)*
In English, being too direct can sometimes sound rude. Fillers help "cushion" the blow.

*Honestly / To be honest:* Used when you’re about to give an opinion or say "no."

"Honestly, I’m not a big fan of that restaurant."

*To be fair:* Used when you are about to present the other side of an argument.

"To be fair, it was his first day on the job."

*Ideally:* Used when describing a perfect (but maybe unrealistic) situation.

"Ideally, I’d like to finish this by Friday."

2. Para suavizar la frase (Politeness Fillers)
Honestly / To be honest: Honestamente / Para ser sincera / La verdad.

Se usa para dar una opinión personal que podría ser negativa o contraria.

To be fair: Para ser justos / Siendo justos.

Se usa cuando vas a defender un punto de vista o justificar a alguien.

Ideally: Idealmente / Lo ideal sería.

Se usa para hablar de un plan perfecto aunque sepas que puede cambiar.

*3. To Check for Understanding*
These keep the listener engaged and confirm they are following you.

*You know? / You know what I mean?:* Often added at the end of a thought.

"It’s just a bit overwhelming, you know?"

*Right?* : Used to get a quick agreement.

"We should probably leave soon, right?"

3. Para confirmar que te siguen (Checking Fillers)
You know? / You know what I mean?: ¿Sabes? / ¿Me entiendes? / ¿Sabes a qué me refiero?

Se usa al final de una frase para buscar la validación del otro.

Right?: ¿Verdad? / ¿No? / ¿Cierto?

Se usa para confirmar un dato rápidamente.
